title: Wood utility poles and reinforcing stubs

definitions.Check: a lengthwise separation of the wood that usually extends across the annual rings, commonly resulting from stresses set up in wood during seasoning.
definitions.Compression wood: abnormal wood usually formed on the lower side of branches and the concave side of leaning trees. Note: It is characterized by an unusually high proportion of apparent latewood in the annual rings, with a gradual transition from earlywood (springwood) to latewood (summerwood). It has a lifeless appearance and exhibits a darker colour when wetted. Compared to normal wood, compression wood shrinks excessively lengthwise. Crack —
definitions.Cross break crack: a separation of the wood cells across the grain. Such breaks can occur when a tree is felled, during handling, or be due to internal strains resulting from unequal longitudinal shrinkage.
definitions.Dead streak: a portion of the sapwood in which the life processes ceased prior to the cutting of the tree. Note: A dead streak differs from a wound such as a scar (cat face) in which the growth of new wood shows that life processes are still acting to repair the injured part. It is characterized by a discoloured, weathered appearance and a lack of growth of healthy wood overlapping the edges of the streak in an attempt to repair the damaged area.
definitions.Decay (rot, dote, doze): the deterioration of wood caused by the action of wood-destroying fungi, resulting in softening, loss of strength and weight, and often change of texture and colour.
definitions.Advanced decay: the late stage of decay in which the decomposition is readily recognized as the wood becomes punky, soft, stringy, pitted, or crumbly.
definitions.Incipient decay: the early stage of decay in which the decomposition has not proceeded far enough to soften or otherwise change the hardness of the wood perceptibly. It is usually accompanied by a slight discoloration or bleaching of the wood. Note: Laboratory analysis may be required for positive identification of incipient decay.
definitions.Face of pole: the concave side of a pole having sweep in one plane or the side of greatest curvature between the groundline and the top of a pole having a reverse or double sweep.
definitions.Groundline section: that section of a pole between 0.305 m (I ft) above and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline as specified in the pole dimension tables of this Standard.
definitions.Hollow heart: a void in the heartwood caused by decay or insect attack.
definitions.Insect damage: damage that is the result of boring in the wood by insects or insect larvae (limits as defined in Clause 4-4.6). that portion of a branch or limb that has been surrounded by a subsequent growth of wood of Knot — the trunk or other portion of the tree.
definitions.Dead knot: a knot resulting from a branch that died before the tree was cut.
definitions.Decayed knot (unsound knot): a knot that is softer than the surrounding wood and shows evidence of advanced decay.
definitions.Knot cluster: two or more knots grouped together as a unit, with the fibres of the wood being deflected around the entire unit; a knot cluster is considered and measured as a single knot.
definitions.Ring knots: a group of knots that encircle a pole in the same plane; any knot intersecting an imaginary line drawn around a pole is included in the measurement of the sum of diameters of ring knots (see Table 1).
definitions.Spike knot: an elongated knot that results from a branch that grew on an angle not perpendicular to the trunk of a tree. Note: Spike knots are often encased in outer bark and/or tree sap, frequently resulting in a bark inclusion (limits as defined in Clause 4.4.8.2).
definitions.Knot diameter: the dimension of a knot measured on the surface of a pole at a right angle to the lengthwise axis of the pole. Note: The sapwood as well as the heartwood portion ofa knot are included in the measurement.
definitions.Mechanical damage: surface damage incurred during the manufacturing or handling of poles.
definitions.Plugged holes: holes that have been filled by forcing in a wood insert.
definitions.Red heart: a form of incipient decay, characterized by a reddish colour produced in the heartwood, that does not render the wood unfit for the majority of uses. Note: Firm red heart contains none of the white pockets that characterize the more advanced stage of decay. It is not to be confused with naturally red heartwood.
definitions.Sap stain: a discoloration of the sapwood that is caused by the action of certain moulds and fungi and is not accompanied by softening or other deterioration of the wood.
definitions.Scar (cat face): a depression in the surface of a pole resulting from a wound where healing has not re- established the normal cross-section of the pole.
definitions.Shake: separation along the grain, the greater part of which occurs between the annual growth rings.
definitions.Short crook: a localized deviation from straightness that, within any section 1.52 m (5 ft) or less in length, is more than one-half the mean diameter of the crooked section (see Figure 2).
definitions.Spiral grain (twisted grain): a type of growth in which the fibres take a spiral course around the trunk of a tree instead of a vertical course. Note: The spiral can extend around the trunk in a right-hand or left-hand direction or can alternate right and left within the trunk. The degree of spirality in a pole is measured by the distance in feet along the axis of the pole in which one complete twist of the spiral occurs.
definitions.Split: a separation along the grain forming an opening or fissure that extends through the piece from one surface to another.
definitions.Sweep: the deviation of a pole from straightness (see Figure I).

Poles shall not be dropped or otherwise roughly handled.
6.7 Storage
When it is necessary to store poles, they shall be stacked on treated skids of such dimensions and
arranged so as to support the poles without producing noticeable distortion in any of them. The height
of the piles shall be limited to avoid damage to poles in the bottom layers. Poles shall be piled and
supported in such a manner that all poles are at least 0.31 m (I ft) above the general ground level. No
vegetation or decaying wood shall be permitted underneath stored poles.
6.8 Inspection
All poles may be subject to inspection by inspectors appointed by the purchaser. Such inspectors shall
have the power to reject any pole that does not comply with the requirements of this Standard.

The fibre stresses are stresses for the purposes of classification and are close approximations to the average bending strengths (MOR) specified in Table
A.I for poles 20 to 35 ft in length.
The bending strengths specified in Table A.I are derived from specimens whose moisture contents at the groundline were above the fibre saturation point
at the time of testing to failure. This condition is recognized as the best approximation for the purposes of this Standard. Furthermore, the average moduli
of elasticity specified in this Table are derived from poles of any length that were unseasoned or completely submerged in water for some time before
testing, as described in the publications referenced in Clause A.9.
The strength of poles longer than 50 ft can be less, as indicated in Annex A.
Fibre stress for several species was based on limited test information or results from one test site; therefore, the Subcommittee is uncertain of the
adequacy of the pole dimensions for these species and recommends that further tests be performed to supplement the database. Notes concerning fibre
stress accompany Tables 3 and E.3.
Other criteria related to the classification of poles are as follows:
a) The taper for determining the circumference at the classification point should be the difference between the minimum top circumference and the
circumference at the theoretical groundline, divided by the length between them.
b) The loading point should be O. 61 m (2 ft) from the pole top.
c) The classification point should be 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt.
d) The term "class" as used in this Standard does not refer to quality limitations or defects ofa pole or reinforcing stub; it is used to differentiate poles
and stubs on the basis of their potential force-resisting capabilities.
Pole test data for yellow cedar, eastern white pine, and ponderosa pine were not available; hence, the values specified in this Table approximate the
average strengths of small, clear bending specimens, as described in the publications referenced in Clause A.9.
Samples of Douglas fir poles taken from coastal areas of British Columbia and from the Cascade Mountains region of Oregon have significantly higher
average strengths than those taken from Rocky Mountain or interior areas. Thus, only Douglas fir poles taken from the western slopes of the Coast and
Cascade Mountains (as defined by the Atlas of Canada and the National Atlas of the United States) shall be classified as coastal Douglas fir. All other
Douglas fir poles shall be classified as interior Douglas fir.

samples taken from various areas of its growth region.
Scots and southern yellow pines are not native to Canada. Southern yellow pine is the name for a commercial grouping of species that includes loblolly
(Pinus taeda), longleaf (P. palustris), shortleaf (P. echinata), and slash (P. elliottii) pines.
Spruce species include black (Picea mariana), Engelmann (P. engelmannii), red (P. rubens), Sitka (P. sitchensis), and white (P. glauca) spruce, of which only
the latter has been tested in a pole size. Separation of red and black spruce from white spruce is impractical once the pole is removed from the forest.
Small, clear bending specimens tested for each species indicate that white spruce is the weakest of the five.

It is recognized that a pole will be stub reinforced usually after it has served a substantial part of its
physical life. Consequently, a stub should have a life at least equal to the remaining life of the pole.
Experience has indicated that this result will generally be met by selecting a reinforcing stub whose

develop the expected remaining strength of a 9.1 (30 ft) Class I pole.

0.title: Introduction
0.text: This Standard covers all commercial pole species used in Canada. Since there is an exchange of poles between Canada, Europe, and the United States, this Standard also includes the imported species of Scots pine and southern yellow pine and harmonizes some of the physical attributes with other countries' standards. During the development of the 2015 edition of this Standard, the Subcommittee agreed that published pole test data sets that are not included in Table A.I of this Standard will be analyzed and, if deemed appropriate, the fibre stress and stiffness of the species in Table 3 Will be updated accordingly in the next edition.

1.1.title: Scope and general application
1.1.text: This Standard covers material, manufacturing, and class dimensional requirements for seasoned wood poles and reinforcing stubs that are primarily intended for the support of electrical power or communication lines.

1.2.title: Structural application exclusions
1.2.text: This Standard does not cover requirements for wood poles intended for use in structures such as bridges and buildings.

1.3.title: Preservative treatment and conditioning
1.3.text: This Standard does not cover requirements for the preservative treatment of poles or the conditioning of poles prior to treatment. Such requirements are detailed in the CAN/CSA-080 Series of Standards unless otherwise specified.

1.4.title: Units of measurement
1.4.text: The values given in SI units are the units of record for the purposes of this Standard. The values given in parentheses are for information and comparison only. Tables I to 23 are written in yard/pound units and equivalent SI (metric) versions are provided in Annex E.

1.5.title: Mandatory language and notes
1.5.text: In this Standard, "shall" is used to express a requirement, i.e., a provision that the user is obliged to satisfy in order to comply with the standard; "should" is used to express a recommendation or that which is advised but not required; and "may" is used to express an option or that which is permissible within the limits of the standard. Notes accompanying clauses do not include requirements or alternative requirements; the purpose of a note accompanying a clause is to separate from the text explanatory or informative material. Notes to tables and figures are considered part of the table or figure and may be written as requirements. Annexes are designated normative (mandatory) or informative (non-mandatory) to define their application.

2.text: This Standard refers to the following publications, and where such reference is made, it shall be to the edition listed below: CSA Group CAN/CSA-080 series-08 (R2012) Wood preservation ANSI (American National Standards Institute) 05.TR.01-2009 Photographic Manual of Wood Pole Characteristics (Based on ANSI 05.1.2008) ASTM International D1036-99(2012) Standard Test Methods of Static Tests of Wood Poles Other publications Natural Resources Canada. The Atlas of Canada. U.S. Department of the Interior. National Atlas of the United States. htt : www.nationalatlas. ov

3.title: Definitions
3.text: The following definitions apply in this Standard. Bird holes — holes and damage caused by woodpeckers and other birds. Check — a lengthwise separation of the wood that usually extends across the annual rings, commonly resulting from stresses set up in wood during seasoning. Compression wood — abnormal wood usually formed on the lower side of branches and the concave side of leaning trees. Note: It is characterized by an unusually high proportion of apparent latewood in the annual rings, with a gradual transition from earlywood (springwood) to latewood (summerwood). It has a lifeless appearance and exhibits a darker colour when wetted. Compared to normal wood, compression wood shrinks excessively lengthwise. Crack — Cross break crack — a separation of the wood cells across the grain. Such breaks can occur when a tree is felled, during handling, or be due to internal strains resulting from unequal longitudinal shrinkage. Dead streak — a portion of the sapwood in which the life processes ceased prior to the cutting of the tree. Note: A dead streak differs from a wound such as a scar (cat face) in which the growth of new wood shows that life processes are still acting to repair the injured part. It is characterized by a discoloured, weathered appearance and a lack of growth of healthy wood overlapping the edges of the streak in an attempt to repair the damaged area. Decay (rot, dote, doze) — the deterioration of wood caused by the action of wood-destroying fungi, resulting in softening, loss of strength and weight, and often change of texture and colour. Advanced decay — the late stage of decay in which the decomposition is readily recognized as the wood becomes punky, soft, stringy, pitted, or crumbly. Incipient decay — the early stage of decay in which the decomposition has not proceeded far enough to soften or otherwise change the hardness of the wood perceptibly. It is usually accompanied by a slight discoloration or bleaching of the wood. Note: Laboratory analysis may be required for positive identification of incipient decay. Face of pole — the concave side of a pole having sweep in one plane or the side of greatest curvature between the groundline and the top of a pole having a reverse or double sweep. Groundline section — that section of a pole between 0.305 m (I ft) above and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline as specified in the pole dimension tables of this Standard. Hollow heart — a void in the heartwood caused by decay or insect attack. Insect damage — damage that is the result of boring in the wood by insects or insect larvae (limits as defined in Clause 4-4.6). that portion of a branch or limb that has been surrounded by a subsequent growth of wood of Knot — the trunk or other portion of the tree. Dead knot — a knot resulting from a branch that died before the tree was cut. Decayed knot (unsound knot) — a knot that is softer than the surrounding wood and shows evidence of advanced decay. Knot cluster — two or more knots grouped together as a unit, with the fibres of the wood being deflected around the entire unit; a knot cluster is considered and measured as a single knot. Ring knots — a group of knots that encircle a pole in the same plane; any knot intersecting an imaginary line drawn around a pole is included in the measurement of the sum of diameters of ring knots (see Table 1). Spike knot — an elongated knot that results from a branch that grew on an angle not perpendicular to the trunk of a tree. Note: Spike knots are often encased in outer bark and/or tree sap, frequently resulting in a bark inclusion (limits as defined in Clause 4.4.8.2). Knot diameter — the dimension of a knot measured on the surface of a pole at a right angle to the lengthwise axis of the pole. Note: The sapwood as well as the heartwood portion ofa knot are included in the measurement. Mechanical damage — surface damage incurred during the manufacturing or handling of poles. Plugged holes — holes that have been filled by forcing in a wood insert. Red heart — a form of incipient decay, characterized by a reddish colour produced in the heartwood, that does not render the wood unfit for the majority of uses. Note: Firm red heart contains none of the white pockets that characterize the more advanced stage of decay. It is not to be confused with naturally red heartwood. Sap stain — a discoloration of the sapwood that is caused by the action of certain moulds and fungi and is not accompanied by softening or other deterioration of the wood. Scar (cat face) — a depression in the surface of a pole resulting from a wound where healing has not re- established the normal cross-section of the pole. Shake — separation along the grain, the greater part of which occurs between the annual growth rings. Short crook — a localized deviation from straightness that, within any section 1.52 m (5 ft) or less in length, is more than one-half the mean diameter of the crooked section (see Figure 2). Spiral grain (twisted grain) — a type of growth in which the fibres take a spiral course around the trunk of a tree instead of a vertical course. Note: The spiral can extend around the trunk in a right-hand or left-hand direction or can alternate right and left within the trunk. The degree of spirality in a pole is measured by the distance in feet along the axis of the pole in which one complete twist of the spiral occurs. Split — a separation along the grain forming an opening or fissure that extends through the piece from one surface to another. Sweep — the deviation of a pole from straightness (see Figure I).

4.1.1.title: Permitted commercial species
4.1.1.text: The species covered by this Standard are listed in Table 3.

4.1.2.title: Classification according to fibre stresses
4.1.2.text: Poles and reinforcing stubs shall be classified in accordance with the circumferential dimensions specified in Tables 4 to 13 and 14 to 23, respectively. These dimensions were calculated from the classification stresses specified in Table 3 in accordance with the classification procedures described in Annexes B and C.

4.1.3.title: Supplier requirements and ordering information
4.1.3.text: Species, length and class of poles, type of preservative treatment, and complete details for boring, gaining, and roofing shall be given to the supplier. Where requirements of this Standard are modified to meet special conditions, complete detailed instructions shall be given to the supplier. See Annex D for ordering information.

4.2.title: Prohibited defects
4.2.text: All poles shall be free of the following defects: a) b) c) d) e) f) g) h) i) j) k) bird holes; cracks; dead streaks, except as permitted in Clause 4.4.3; decay, except as permitted by Clauses 4.4.4 and 4.4.5; double sweep or reverse sweep in reinforcing stubs (see Clause 4.4.12); plugged holes, except increment borer holes; hollow heart in butts or tops, except as permitted by Clause 4.4.5; marine borer damage; nails, spikes, and other metal not specifically authorized by the purchaser; short crook (see Clause 4.4.12); and splits in the top.

4.3.title: Permitted defects
4.3.text: The following defects shall be permitted: a) checks that result from normal seasoning conditions and that extend not deeper than the depth of pith (see Clause 4.4.1 for limitations on two or more checks that become contiguous at the pith); b) fire-kill, provided that there is no char; c) firm red heart; and d) sap stain that is not accompanied by decay.

4.4.1.title: Contiguous checks, through-checks, and splits
4.4.1.text: Contiguous checks, through-checks, or splits in the butt surface shall be permitted, provided that their height from the butt along the side surface does not exceed 0.61 m (2 ft).

4.4.2.title: Compression wood
4.4.2.text: The outer 2.54 cm (1 in) of all poles shall be free of compression wood visible on either end.

4.4.3.title: Dead streaks
4.4.3.text: A single sound dead streak, not wider than one-quarter of the circumference of the pole measured at the widest point of the dead streak, shall be permitted in cedar poles only.

4.4.4.title: Decay in knots
4.4.4.text: Decay shall be permitted in knots, provided that it is not associated with heart rot.

4.4.5.title: Defective butts
4.4.5.text: Hollowing of the butt caused by "splinter pulling" in felling the tree shall be permitted, provided that the area of such a hollow is less than 10% of the butt area. Hollow heart and decay shall be permitted in cedar poles only, provided that the aggregate area of hollow heart and decay does not exceed 10% of the butt area and that the depth of the hollow does not exceed 0.61 m (2 ft), measured from the butt surface. Decay in the butt within 5.1 cm (2 in) of the pole surface shall be permitted in cedar poles only, provided that the total area of decay does not exceed 6.45 cm2 (I in2).

4.4.6.title: Insect damage
4.4.6.text: Insect damage consisting of holes 1.6 mm (1/16 in) or less in diameter shall be permitted. Surface scoring or channelling shall be permitted. All other forms of insect damage shall be prohibited.

4.4.7.title: Knot diameter
4.4.7.text: The diameter of any single knot or the sum of the diameters of all knots in any 0.305 m (1 ft) section shall not exceed the limits specified in Table 1. Knots 13 mm (1/2 in) or less in diameter shall be ignored in applying the limitations for the sum of diameters. The diameter of any single knot is measured at the widest point of the knot, perpendicular to the length of the pole, and includes the sapwood and heartwood of the knot, as shown in Figure 3.

4.4.8.1.title: Sound scars
4.4.8.1.text: Sound scars shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) b) c) d) e) they are not located within 0.61 m (2 ft) of the groundline; they are smoothly trimmed and do not interfere with the cutting of any gain or drilled hole; the circumference of any point on the trimmed surfaces located between the butt and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline is not less than the minimum circumference specified at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt for the class and length of the pole; the maximum width of the scar, after trimming, is not more than one-fifth of the pole circumference at that point; and the maximum depth of the trimmed scar (bark removed) is not more than i) 25 mm (1 in) if the pole diameter at the location of the scar is 0.25 m (10 in) or less; or ii) one-tenth of the pole diameter at the location of the scar if such diameter is more than 0.25 m (IO in).

4.4.8.2.title: Bark inclusions
4.4.8.2.text: Sound bark inclusions, bark removed, shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) they are not located within 0.61 m (2 ft) of the groundline; and b) the depth of the bark inclusion (bark removed) does not exceed i) one-fifth of the pole diameter at the bark inclusion if the inclusion is 20.3 cm (8 in) or less in length; or ii) 2.5 cm (1 in) if the inclusion is more than 20.3 cm (8 in) long.

4.4.8.3.title: Mechanical damage
4.4.8.3.text: Mechanical damage shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) b) c) d) e) they are not located within two feet of the groundline; damage over 1.3 cm (h in) in depth is smoothly trimmed and shaped to remove all broken and splintered fibre; the circumference of any point on the trimmed surfaces located between the butt and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline is not less than the minimum circumference specified at 6 ft from the butt for the class and length of the pole; the maximum width of the damage, after trimming, is not more than one-fifth of the pole circumference at that point; and the maximum depth of the trimmed damage is not more than i) 25 mm (1 in) if the pole diameter at the location of the scar is 0.25 m (10 in) or less; or ii) one-tenth of the pole diameter at the location of the damage if such diameter is more than 0.25 m (10 in).

4.4.9.title: Shakes in butts
4.4.9.text: Shakes in the butt end surface extending through an arc of not more than 900 shall be permitted. Shakes extending through an arc of more than 900 shall be permitted if they are inside a circle, the centre of which corresponds to the centre of the butt surface and the diameter of which corresponds to one-half of the average butt diameter.

4.4.10.title: Shakes in tops
4.4.10.text: Shakes in the top end surface shall be permitted in poles that are to be given full-length preservative treatment, provided that the diameter of the shake does not exceed one-half of the diameter of the top of the pole.

4.4.11.title: Spiral grain
4.4.11.text: Spiral grain (twist grain) shall be permitted within the limits specified in Table 2.

4.4.12.title: Crooks and sweep
4.4.12.text: Crooks other than short crooks shall be permitted in poles. Sweep shall be permitted, provided that a straight line connecting the midpoint at the groundline with the midpoint at the top shall not, at any intermediate point, pass through the surface of the pole. Double or reverse sweep shall not be permitted in reinforcing stubs. (See Figures I and 2.)

4.4.13.1.title: Douglas fir and western larch rate of growth
4.4.13.1.text: Except as specified in Clause 4.4.13.2, the rate of growth measured on the butt in the outer 51 mm (2 in) of poles having a circumference of 0.95 m (37.5 in) or less at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, and in the outer 76 mm (3 in) of poles having a circumference of more than 0.95 m (37.5 in) at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, shall be not less than 6 rings per 2.54 cm (1 in).

4.4.13.2.title: Southern yellow pine rate of growth
4.4.13.2.text: Poles with 4 and 5 rings per 2.54 cm (1 in) shall be acceptable if 50% or more summerwood is present.

4.4.13.3.title: Scots pine rate of growth
4.4.13.3.text: As an alternative to Clause 4.4.13.1, the ring count and summerwood measurements may be made on an increment core taken at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt directly above the place where the average growth is indicated on the butt surface. Note: ANSI 05. TR.OI provides accurate photographic references for the limited and prohibited defects noted in this Standard.

5.1.1.title: General
5.1.1.text: Poles shall be classified according to species, length, and minimum circumferential measurements as specified in Tables 4 to 13.

5.1.2.title: Length
5.1.2.text: Poles 45 ft in length or shorter shall be not more than 76 mm (3 in) shorter or 76 mm (3 in) longer than the nominal length. Poles 15.24 m (50 ft) or more in length shall be not more than 76 mm (3 in) shorter or 152 mm (6 in) longer than the nominal length. Length shall be measured between the extreme ends of the pole.

5.1.3.title: Circumference
5.1.3.text: The minimum circumferences at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt and at the top, for each length and class of pole, are listed in Tables 4 to 13. The circumference at 1.83 (6 ft) from the butt of a pole shall be not more than 178 mm (7 in) or 20% larger than the specified minimum, whichever is greater. The top circumferential requirement shall apply at a point corresponding to the minimum length permitted for the pole.

5.1.4.title: Classification method
5.1.4.text: After the species and length of a pole are determined, its class shall be determined by measuring circumferences at two cross-sections: the top and 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt. The latter dimension shall determine the class of the pole by reference to the applicable table in Tables 4 to 13, provided that its top (measured at the minimum length point) is large enough. Otherwise, the circumference at the top shall determine the class, provided that the circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt does not exceed the specified minimum by more than 178 mm (7 in) or 20%, whichever is greater.

5.2.title: Reinforcing stub circumference
5.2.text: The minimum circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, for each length and class of stub, shall be as specified in Tables 14 to 23.

6.title: Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

6.1.title: Bark removal
6.1.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

6.1.1.title: Outer bark removal and inner bark limits
6.1.1.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.1.1.text: The outer bark shall be completely removed from all poles. No patch of inner bark more than 25 mm (1 in) wide and 152 mm (6 in) long shall be left on the pole surface between the top and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline.

6.1.2.title: Shaving depth of cut
6.1.2.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.1.2.text: In shaving poles, the depth of cut shall be not more than necessary to remove inner bark. There shall be no abrupt changes in the contour of the pole surface between the groundline and top sections.

6.2.title: Sawing
6.2.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.2.text: Poles shall be sawed neatly at the top and at the butt along planes that shall not be out of square with the axis of the pole by more than 10% of the diameter of the sawed surface. There may be bevelling at the edge of the sawed butt surface not wider than 10% of the butt diameter.

6.3.title: Trimming
6.3.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.3.text: Completely overgrown knots rising more than 25 mm (1 in) above the pole surface, branch stubs, and partially overgrown knots shall be trimmed close. Completely overgrown knots less than 25 mm (1 in) high need not be trimmed.

6.4.title: Framing
6.4.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.4.text: All poles shall be roofed, gained, and bored as specified by the purchaser before full-length treatment. All gains of a notch or slab type shall be cut on the face of the pole, and the gained surfaces shall be in parallel planes.

6.5.title: Markings
6.5.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

6.5.1.title: Butt marking
6.5.1.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.5.1.text: The following marks shall be stamped or branded legibly on the butt end of each pole or be included on a metal tag affixed thereto: a) the supplier's code or trademark; b) code letters denoting the pole species (see Clause 6.5.3); and c) the class and length of the pole. Marks stamped or branded on the butt end shall be not less than 16 mm (5/8 in) high. Marks on metal tags shall be not less than 3.2 mm (1/8) in high.

6.5.2.title: Side marking
6.5.2.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

6.5.2.1.title: Side marking location
6.5.2.1.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.5.2.1.text: Not more than one month before treatment, the following marks, not less than 16 mm (5/8) in high, shall be branded legibly and permanently on the face of each pole: the supplier's code or trademark; b) the plant location and the last two numerals of the year of treatment; c) code letters denoting the country of origin (for imported poles) and pole species (see Clause 6.5.3); d) the class and length of the pole; and e) following the species code letters [see Item c)], the appropriate code letter to denote the type of preservative, as specified in the CAN/CSA-080 Series of Standards. Note: Subject to agreement between the supplier and purchaser, die-stamped metal tags affixed to the pole face may be used in place of brands to designate side marking information. If metal tags are used, the code letters specified in Item c) should be not less than 1/8 in high.

6.5.2.2.title: Side marking code layout
6.5.2.2.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.5.2.2.text: The bottom of the side mark shall be located on the face of the pole at 3.05 m ± 0.05 m (IO ft ± 2 in) from the butt of poles 15.2 m (50 ft) or less in length, and at 4.27 m ± 0.05 m (14 ft ± 2 in) from the butt of poles 16.8 m (55 ft) or more in length. In the case of 3.05 m (10 ft), 3.35 m (11 ft), and 3.96 m (13 ft) stubs, the mark should be 0.31 m (1 ft) from the top.

6.5.3.title: Code letters for country of origin and pole species
6.5.3.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.5.3.text: The following code letters shall be used to designate the country of origin of an imported pole and the species of pole. The code letter for the country of origin shall precede the code letters for the species on all imported poles except those of southern yellow pine: Country of origin Finland Norway Sweden United States Code letter s- Species Cedar Eastern white Western red Yellow Fir Amabilis Douglas Hemlock Western Larch western Pine Eastern white Jack Lodgepole Ponderosa Red Scots Southern yellow Spruce Black Engelmann Red Sitka White Code letters EC wc YC WH WL pp scp ws ES ss

6.6.title: Handling of poles and reinforcing stubs
6.6.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

6.6.1.title: Handling equipment restrictions
6.6.1.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.6.1.text: Treated material shall not be dragged along the ground.

6.6.2.title: Treated pole surface protection
6.6.2.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.6.2.text: Cant hooks, pole tongs, or other tools shall not be applied to the groundline section of any pole.

6.6.3.title: Loading irons and cant hooks restriction
6.6.3.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.6.3.text: Loading irons and cant hooks shall not be used on the roofed surface of any pole.

6.6.4.title: Rough handling prohibition
6.6.4.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.6.4.text: Poles shall not be dropped or otherwise roughly handled.

6.7.title: Storage
6.7.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.7.text: When it is necessary to store poles, they shall be stacked on treated skids of such dimensions and arranged so as to support the poles without producing noticeable distortion in any of them. The height of the piles shall be limited to avoid damage to poles in the bottom layers. Poles shall be piled and supported in such a manner that all poles are at least 0.31 m (I ft) above the general ground level. No vegetation or decaying wood shall be permitted underneath stored poles.

6.8.title: Inspection
6.8.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
6.8.text: All poles may be subject to inspection by inspectors appointed by the purchaser. Such inspectors shall have the power to reject any pole that does not comply with the requirements of this Standard.

A.1.title: Objective
A.1.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
A.1.text: The objective of this Annex is to present a database for classification stresses (see Table A.I) considered to be representative of material that is available to the Canadian market.

A.2.title: Definitions

A.3.title: Strength determination
A.3.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
A.3.text: A reasonable estimate of the percentage of a sample of poles having strengths falling within a specific range can be obtained using normal probability theory. On this basis, the range expressed by ± 1 standard deviation from the average value will Include about 68% of cases, ± 2 standard deviations from the average will include about 95% of cases, and ± 3 standard deviations from the average will include about 99.7% of cases. Thus, from a sample of poles having an average modulus of rupture of 552 bar (8000 psi) and a standard deviation of 69 bar (1000 psi), the strengths of 68% of the sample can be expected to fall within the range of 483 to 621 bar (7000 to 9000 psi), 95% within the range of 414 to 690 bar (6000 to 10 000 psi), and 99.7% within the range of 345 to 758 bar (5000 to 11 000 psi).

A.4.title: Coefficient of variation
A.4.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses

A.6.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
A.6.text: The moisture content of most specimens when tested was above the fibre saturation point, as required by ASTM [)1036, which has been used since 1949 for the testing of utility poles. The fibre saturation point is the moisture content level at which swelling of the wood ceases or shrinkage begins. A moisture content above the fibre saturation point is a condition at the groundline recognized as the best approximation for the purposes of this Standard.

B.1.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles

B.1.1.title: Calculation of minimum circumferences and horizontal loads
B.1.1.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
B.1.1.text: The minimum circumferences specified in Tables 4 to 13 have been calculated in order for each species in a given class to develop groundline stresses approximately equal to those specified in Table 3 when a given horizontal load is applied 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top of the pole. The horizontal loads used in the calculations for separating the thirteen classes are specified in Table B.I.

B.1.2.title: Cantilever groundline stress assumptions and taper calculation
B.1.2.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
B.1.2.text: In making the calculations, it was assumed that the pole is used as a simple cantilever and that the maximum fibre stress in the pole subjected to the bending moment applied will occur at the groundline. The circumference at the groundline was calculated using the standard engineering formula. This value was then used to calculate the required circumference 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt using a calculated taper per foot of length between the groundline and 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt. The calculated circumference 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt was rounded to the nearest 13 mm (1/2 in). Note: A calculated taper is the difference between the minimum top circumference and the groundline circumference divided by the length between them.

B.1.3.title: Theoretical groundline vs above groundline maximum stress
B.1.3.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
B.1.3.text: The assumption that the maximum fibre stress in the pole occurs at the groundline is theoretically correct, provided that the circumference at the groundline is not more than 1-1/2 times the circumference at the point of loading. If the circumference at the groundline is more than 1-1/2 times the circumference at the point of loading, theoretically the maximum fibre stress in the pole occurs above the groundline at the point where the circumference is 1-1/2 times that at the point of loading (not necessarily the circumference 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top). When the load is not applied 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top, it is necessary for the class of pole to be determined by making separate calculations from the specific loads to be supported. Unless other information is available to substantiate the actual taper of the pole for a given species, these calculations should be based on the taper determined by the difference in circumference between the specified top dimension and the groundline dimension divided by the distance in feet between the two measurements.

B.2.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles

clause_list.title: Introduction
clause_list.text: This Standard covers all commercial pole species used in Canada. Since there is an exchange of poles between Canada, Europe, and the United States, this Standard also includes the imported species of Scots pine and southern yellow pine and harmonizes some of the physical attributes with other countries' standards. During the development of the 2015 edition of this Standard, the Subcommittee agreed that published pole test data sets that are not included in Table A.I of this Standard will be analyzed and, if deemed appropriate, the fibre stress and stiffness of the species in Table 3 Will be updated accordingly in the next edition.

clause_list.title: Scope and general application
clause_list.text: This Standard covers material, manufacturing, and class dimensional requirements for seasoned wood poles and reinforcing stubs that are primarily intended for the support of electrical power or communication lines.

clause_list.title: Structural application exclusions
clause_list.text: This Standard does not cover requirements for wood poles intended for use in structures such as bridges and buildings.

clause_list.title: Preservative treatment and conditioning
clause_list.text: This Standard does not cover requirements for the preservative treatment of poles or the conditioning of poles prior to treatment. Such requirements are detailed in the CAN/CSA-080 Series of Standards unless otherwise specified.

clause_list.title: Units of measurement
clause_list.text: The values given in SI units are the units of record for the purposes of this Standard. The values given in parentheses are for information and comparison only. Tables I to 23 are written in yard/pound units and equivalent SI (metric) versions are provided in Annex E.

clause_list.title: Mandatory language and notes
clause_list.text: In this Standard, "shall" is used to express a requirement, i.e., a provision that the user is obliged to satisfy in order to comply with the standard; "should" is used to express a recommendation or that which is advised but not required; and "may" is used to express an option or that which is permissible within the limits of the standard. Notes accompanying clauses do not include requirements or alternative requirements; the purpose of a note accompanying a clause is to separate from the text explanatory or informative material. Notes to tables and figures are considered part of the table or figure and may be written as requirements. Annexes are designated normative (mandatory) or informative (non-mandatory) to define their application.

clause_list.title: Definitions
clause_list.text: The following definitions apply in this Standard. Bird holes — holes and damage caused by woodpeckers and other birds. Check — a lengthwise separation of the wood that usually extends across the annual rings, commonly resulting from stresses set up in wood during seasoning. Compression wood — abnormal wood usually formed on the lower side of branches and the concave side of leaning trees. Note: It is characterized by an unusually high proportion of apparent latewood in the annual rings, with a gradual transition from earlywood (springwood) to latewood (summerwood). It has a lifeless appearance and exhibits a darker colour when wetted. Compared to normal wood, compression wood shrinks excessively lengthwise. Crack — Cross break crack — a separation of the wood cells across the grain. Such breaks can occur when a tree is felled, during handling, or be due to internal strains resulting from unequal longitudinal shrinkage. Dead streak — a portion of the sapwood in which the life processes ceased prior to the cutting of the tree. Note: A dead streak differs from a wound such as a scar (cat face) in which the growth of new wood shows that life processes are still acting to repair the injured part. It is characterized by a discoloured, weathered appearance and a lack of growth of healthy wood overlapping the edges of the streak in an attempt to repair the damaged area. Decay (rot, dote, doze) — the deterioration of wood caused by the action of wood-destroying fungi, resulting in softening, loss of strength and weight, and often change of texture and colour. Advanced decay — the late stage of decay in which the decomposition is readily recognized as the wood becomes punky, soft, stringy, pitted, or crumbly. Incipient decay — the early stage of decay in which the decomposition has not proceeded far enough to soften or otherwise change the hardness of the wood perceptibly. It is usually accompanied by a slight discoloration or bleaching of the wood. Note: Laboratory analysis may be required for positive identification of incipient decay. Face of pole — the concave side of a pole having sweep in one plane or the side of greatest curvature between the groundline and the top of a pole having a reverse or double sweep. Groundline section — that section of a pole between 0.305 m (I ft) above and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline as specified in the pole dimension tables of this Standard. Hollow heart — a void in the heartwood caused by decay or insect attack. Insect damage — damage that is the result of boring in the wood by insects or insect larvae (limits as defined in Clause 4-4.6). that portion of a branch or limb that has been surrounded by a subsequent growth of wood of Knot — the trunk or other portion of the tree. Dead knot — a knot resulting from a branch that died before the tree was cut. Decayed knot (unsound knot) — a knot that is softer than the surrounding wood and shows evidence of advanced decay. Knot cluster — two or more knots grouped together as a unit, with the fibres of the wood being deflected around the entire unit; a knot cluster is considered and measured as a single knot. Ring knots — a group of knots that encircle a pole in the same plane; any knot intersecting an imaginary line drawn around a pole is included in the measurement of the sum of diameters of ring knots (see Table 1). Spike knot — an elongated knot that results from a branch that grew on an angle not perpendicular to the trunk of a tree. Note: Spike knots are often encased in outer bark and/or tree sap, frequently resulting in a bark inclusion (limits as defined in Clause 4.4.8.2). Knot diameter — the dimension of a knot measured on the surface of a pole at a right angle to the lengthwise axis of the pole. Note: The sapwood as well as the heartwood portion ofa knot are included in the measurement. Mechanical damage — surface damage incurred during the manufacturing or handling of poles. Plugged holes — holes that have been filled by forcing in a wood insert. Red heart — a form of incipient decay, characterized by a reddish colour produced in the heartwood, that does not render the wood unfit for the majority of uses. Note: Firm red heart contains none of the white pockets that characterize the more advanced stage of decay. It is not to be confused with naturally red heartwood. Sap stain — a discoloration of the sapwood that is caused by the action of certain moulds and fungi and is not accompanied by softening or other deterioration of the wood. Scar (cat face) — a depression in the surface of a pole resulting from a wound where healing has not re- established the normal cross-section of the pole. Shake — separation along the grain, the greater part of which occurs between the annual growth rings. Short crook — a localized deviation from straightness that, within any section 1.52 m (5 ft) or less in length, is more than one-half the mean diameter of the crooked section (see Figure 2). Spiral grain (twisted grain) — a type of growth in which the fibres take a spiral course around the trunk of a tree instead of a vertical course. Note: The spiral can extend around the trunk in a right-hand or left-hand direction or can alternate right and left within the trunk. The degree of spirality in a pole is measured by the distance in feet along the axis of the pole in which one complete twist of the spiral occurs. Split — a separation along the grain forming an opening or fissure that extends through the piece from one surface to another. Sweep — the deviation of a pole from straightness (see Figure I).

clause_list.text: The species covered by this Standard are listed in Table 3.

clause_list.title: Classification according to fibre stresses
clause_list.text: Poles and reinforcing stubs shall be classified in accordance with the circumferential dimensions specified in Tables 4 to 13 and 14 to 23, respectively. These dimensions were calculated from the classification stresses specified in Table 3 in accordance with the classification procedures described in Annexes B and C.

clause_list.title: Supplier requirements and ordering information
clause_list.text: Species, length and class of poles, type of preservative treatment, and complete details for boring, gaining, and roofing shall be given to the supplier. Where requirements of this Standard are modified to meet special conditions, complete detailed instructions shall be given to the supplier. See Annex D for ordering information.

clause_list.title: Prohibited defects
clause_list.text: All poles shall be free of the following defects: a) b) c) d) e) f) g) h) i) j) k) bird holes; cracks; dead streaks, except as permitted in Clause 4.4.3; decay, except as permitted by Clauses 4.4.4 and 4.4.5; double sweep or reverse sweep in reinforcing stubs (see Clause 4.4.12); plugged holes, except increment borer holes; hollow heart in butts or tops, except as permitted by Clause 4.4.5; marine borer damage; nails, spikes, and other metal not specifically authorized by the purchaser; short crook (see Clause 4.4.12); and splits in the top.

clause_list.title: Permitted defects
clause_list.text: The following defects shall be permitted: a) checks that result from normal seasoning conditions and that extend not deeper than the depth of pith (see Clause 4.4.1 for limitations on two or more checks that become contiguous at the pith); b) fire-kill, provided that there is no char; c) firm red heart; and d) sap stain that is not accompanied by decay.

clause_list.title: Contiguous checks, through-checks, and splits
clause_list.text: Contiguous checks, through-checks, or splits in the butt surface shall be permitted, provided that their height from the butt along the side surface does not exceed 0.61 m (2 ft).

clause_list.title: Compression wood
clause_list.text: The outer 2.54 cm (1 in) of all poles shall be free of compression wood visible on either end.

clause_list.title: Dead streaks
clause_list.text: A single sound dead streak, not wider than one-quarter of the circumference of the pole measured at the widest point of the dead streak, shall be permitted in cedar poles only.

clause_list.title: Decay in knots
clause_list.text: Decay shall be permitted in knots, provided that it is not associated with heart rot.

clause_list.title: Defective butts
clause_list.text: Hollowing of the butt caused by "splinter pulling" in felling the tree shall be permitted, provided that the area of such a hollow is less than 10% of the butt area. Hollow heart and decay shall be permitted in cedar poles only, provided that the aggregate area of hollow heart and decay does not exceed 10% of the butt area and that the depth of the hollow does not exceed 0.61 m (2 ft), measured from the butt surface. Decay in the butt within 5.1 cm (2 in) of the pole surface shall be permitted in cedar poles only, provided that the total area of decay does not exceed 6.45 cm2 (I in2).

clause_list.title: Insect damage
clause_list.text: Insect damage consisting of holes 1.6 mm (1/16 in) or less in diameter shall be permitted. Surface scoring or channelling shall be permitted. All other forms of insect damage shall be prohibited.

clause_list.title: Knot diameter
clause_list.text: The diameter of any single knot or the sum of the diameters of all knots in any 0.305 m (1 ft) section shall not exceed the limits specified in Table 1. Knots 13 mm (1/2 in) or less in diameter shall be ignored in applying the limitations for the sum of diameters. The diameter of any single knot is measured at the widest point of the knot, perpendicular to the length of the pole, and includes the sapwood and heartwood of the knot, as shown in Figure 3.

clause_list.title: Sound scars
clause_list.text: Sound scars shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) b) c) d) e) they are not located within 0.61 m (2 ft) of the groundline; they are smoothly trimmed and do not interfere with the cutting of any gain or drilled hole; the circumference of any point on the trimmed surfaces located between the butt and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline is not less than the minimum circumference specified at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt for the class and length of the pole; the maximum width of the scar, after trimming, is not more than one-fifth of the pole circumference at that point; and the maximum depth of the trimmed scar (bark removed) is not more than i) 25 mm (1 in) if the pole diameter at the location of the scar is 0.25 m (10 in) or less; or ii) one-tenth of the pole diameter at the location of the scar if such diameter is more than 0.25 m (IO in).

clause_list.title: Bark inclusions
clause_list.text: Sound bark inclusions, bark removed, shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) they are not located within 0.61 m (2 ft) of the groundline; and b) the depth of the bark inclusion (bark removed) does not exceed i) one-fifth of the pole diameter at the bark inclusion if the inclusion is 20.3 cm (8 in) or less in length; or ii) 2.5 cm (1 in) if the inclusion is more than 20.3 cm (8 in) long.

clause_list.title: Mechanical damage
clause_list.text: Mechanical damage shall be permitted on a pole surface, provided that a) b) c) d) e) they are not located within two feet of the groundline; damage over 1.3 cm (h in) in depth is smoothly trimmed and shaped to remove all broken and splintered fibre; the circumference of any point on the trimmed surfaces located between the butt and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline is not less than the minimum circumference specified at 6 ft from the butt for the class and length of the pole; the maximum width of the damage, after trimming, is not more than one-fifth of the pole circumference at that point; and the maximum depth of the trimmed damage is not more than i) 25 mm (1 in) if the pole diameter at the location of the scar is 0.25 m (10 in) or less; or ii) one-tenth of the pole diameter at the location of the damage if such diameter is more than 0.25 m (10 in).

clause_list.title: Shakes in butts
clause_list.text: Shakes in the butt end surface extending through an arc of not more than 900 shall be permitted. Shakes extending through an arc of more than 900 shall be permitted if they are inside a circle, the centre of which corresponds to the centre of the butt surface and the diameter of which corresponds to one-half of the average butt diameter.

clause_list.title: Shakes in tops
clause_list.text: Shakes in the top end surface shall be permitted in poles that are to be given full-length preservative treatment, provided that the diameter of the shake does not exceed one-half of the diameter of the top of the pole.

clause_list.title: Spiral grain
clause_list.text: Spiral grain (twist grain) shall be permitted within the limits specified in Table 2.

clause_list.title: Crooks and sweep
clause_list.text: Crooks other than short crooks shall be permitted in poles. Sweep shall be permitted, provided that a straight line connecting the midpoint at the groundline with the midpoint at the top shall not, at any intermediate point, pass through the surface of the pole. Double or reverse sweep shall not be permitted in reinforcing stubs. (See Figures I and 2.)

clause_list.title: Douglas fir and western larch rate of growth
clause_list.text: Except as specified in Clause 4.4.13.2, the rate of growth measured on the butt in the outer 51 mm (2 in) of poles having a circumference of 0.95 m (37.5 in) or less at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, and in the outer 76 mm (3 in) of poles having a circumference of more than 0.95 m (37.5 in) at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, shall be not less than 6 rings per 2.54 cm (1 in).

clause_list.title: Southern yellow pine rate of growth
clause_list.text: Poles with 4 and 5 rings per 2.54 cm (1 in) shall be acceptable if 50% or more summerwood is present.

clause_list.title: Scots pine rate of growth
clause_list.text: As an alternative to Clause 4.4.13.1, the ring count and summerwood measurements may be made on an increment core taken at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt directly above the place where the average growth is indicated on the butt surface. Note: ANSI 05. TR.OI provides accurate photographic references for the limited and prohibited defects noted in this Standard.

clause_list.title: General
clause_list.text: Poles shall be classified according to species, length, and minimum circumferential measurements as specified in Tables 4 to 13.

clause_list.title: Length
clause_list.text: Poles 45 ft in length or shorter shall be not more than 76 mm (3 in) shorter or 76 mm (3 in) longer than the nominal length. Poles 15.24 m (50 ft) or more in length shall be not more than 76 mm (3 in) shorter or 152 mm (6 in) longer than the nominal length. Length shall be measured between the extreme ends of the pole.

clause_list.title: Circumference
clause_list.text: The minimum circumferences at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt and at the top, for each length and class of pole, are listed in Tables 4 to 13. The circumference at 1.83 (6 ft) from the butt of a pole shall be not more than 178 mm (7 in) or 20% larger than the specified minimum, whichever is greater. The top circumferential requirement shall apply at a point corresponding to the minimum length permitted for the pole.

clause_list.title: Classification method
clause_list.text: After the species and length of a pole are determined, its class shall be determined by measuring circumferences at two cross-sections: the top and 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt. The latter dimension shall determine the class of the pole by reference to the applicable table in Tables 4 to 13, provided that its top (measured at the minimum length point) is large enough. Otherwise, the circumference at the top shall determine the class, provided that the circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt does not exceed the specified minimum by more than 178 mm (7 in) or 20%, whichever is greater.

clause_list.title: Reinforcing stub circumference
clause_list.text: The minimum circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt, for each length and class of stub, shall be as specified in Tables 14 to 23.

clause_list.title: Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

clause_list.title: Bark removal
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

clause_list.title: Outer bark removal and inner bark limits
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: The outer bark shall be completely removed from all poles. No patch of inner bark more than 25 mm (1 in) wide and 152 mm (6 in) long shall be left on the pole surface between the top and 0.61 m (2 ft) below the groundline.

clause_list.title: Shaving depth of cut
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: In shaving poles, the depth of cut shall be not more than necessary to remove inner bark. There shall be no abrupt changes in the contour of the pole surface between the groundline and top sections.

clause_list.title: Sawing
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Poles shall be sawed neatly at the top and at the butt along planes that shall not be out of square with the axis of the pole by more than 10% of the diameter of the sawed surface. There may be bevelling at the edge of the sawed butt surface not wider than 10% of the butt diameter.

clause_list.title: Trimming
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Completely overgrown knots rising more than 25 mm (1 in) above the pole surface, branch stubs, and partially overgrown knots shall be trimmed close. Completely overgrown knots less than 25 mm (1 in) high need not be trimmed.

clause_list.title: Framing
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: All poles shall be roofed, gained, and bored as specified by the purchaser before full-length treatment. All gains of a notch or slab type shall be cut on the face of the pole, and the gained surfaces shall be in parallel planes.

clause_list.title: Markings
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

clause_list.title: Butt marking
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: The following marks shall be stamped or branded legibly on the butt end of each pole or be included on a metal tag affixed thereto: a) the supplier's code or trademark; b) code letters denoting the pole species (see Clause 6.5.3); and c) the class and length of the pole. Marks stamped or branded on the butt end shall be not less than 16 mm (5/8 in) high. Marks on metal tags shall be not less than 3.2 mm (1/8) in high.

clause_list.title: Side marking
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

clause_list.title: Side marking location
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Not more than one month before treatment, the following marks, not less than 16 mm (5/8) in high, shall be branded legibly and permanently on the face of each pole: the supplier's code or trademark; b) the plant location and the last two numerals of the year of treatment; c) code letters denoting the country of origin (for imported poles) and pole species (see Clause 6.5.3); d) the class and length of the pole; and e) following the species code letters [see Item c)], the appropriate code letter to denote the type of preservative, as specified in the CAN/CSA-080 Series of Standards. Note: Subject to agreement between the supplier and purchaser, die-stamped metal tags affixed to the pole face may be used in place of brands to designate side marking information. If metal tags are used, the code letters specified in Item c) should be not less than 1/8 in high.

clause_list.title: Side marking code layout
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: The bottom of the side mark shall be located on the face of the pole at 3.05 m ± 0.05 m (IO ft ± 2 in) from the butt of poles 15.2 m (50 ft) or less in length, and at 4.27 m ± 0.05 m (14 ft ± 2 in) from the butt of poles 16.8 m (55 ft) or more in length. In the case of 3.05 m (10 ft), 3.35 m (11 ft), and 3.96 m (13 ft) stubs, the mark should be 0.31 m (1 ft) from the top.

clause_list.title: Code letters for country of origin and pole species
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: The following code letters shall be used to designate the country of origin of an imported pole and the species of pole. The code letter for the country of origin shall precede the code letters for the species on all imported poles except those of southern yellow pine: Country of origin Finland Norway Sweden United States Code letter s- Species Cedar Eastern white Western red Yellow Fir Amabilis Douglas Hemlock Western Larch western Pine Eastern white Jack Lodgepole Ponderosa Red Scots Southern yellow Spruce Black Engelmann Red Sitka White Code letters EC wc YC WH WL pp scp ws ES ss

clause_list.title: Handling of poles and reinforcing stubs
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection

clause_list.title: Handling equipment restrictions
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Treated material shall not be dragged along the ground.

clause_list.title: Treated pole surface protection
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Cant hooks, pole tongs, or other tools shall not be applied to the groundline section of any pole.

clause_list.title: Loading irons and cant hooks restriction
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Loading irons and cant hooks shall not be used on the roofed surface of any pole.

clause_list.title: Rough handling prohibition
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: Poles shall not be dropped or otherwise roughly handled.

clause_list.title: Storage
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: When it is necessary to store poles, they shall be stacked on treated skids of such dimensions and arranged so as to support the poles without producing noticeable distortion in any of them. The height of the piles shall be limited to avoid damage to poles in the bottom layers. Poles shall be piled and supported in such a manner that all poles are at least 0.31 m (I ft) above the general ground level. No vegetation or decaying wood shall be permitted underneath stored poles.

clause_list.title: Inspection
clause_list.section: 6 Quality of work and finish, markings, handling, storage, and inspection
clause_list.text: All poles may be subject to inspection by inspectors appointed by the purchaser. Such inspectors shall have the power to reject any pole that does not comply with the requirements of this Standard.

clause_list.title: Objective
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: The objective of this Annex is to present a database for classification stresses (see Table A.I) considered to be representative of material that is available to the Canadian market.

clause_list.title: Definitions
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: The following definitions apply in this Annex: Note: The following definitions provide a guide to the column headings in Table A.I. The abbreviations in parentheses following the defined terms reflect the abbreviations in the column headings. See also Note 4) to Table A.I. Length — the nominal length of poles in the sample. The testing span is smaller and generally in accordance with ASTM D1036. Modulus of elasticity (MOE) — the average modulus of elasticity in 69 bar (103 lbs/in2) units calculated, in most cases, in accordance with ASTM D1036. Modulus of rupture (MOR) — the average modulus of rupture or maximum breaking stress in pounds per square inch. Note: Users should not infer that all poles broke at the groundline. Many broke at a smaller cross-section where the calculated extreme fibre stress was usually less, but might have been greater, than that at the groundline cross-section. Reference number (Ref. no.) — the number assigned in this Annex's bibliography (see Clause A.9) to the document on which the related information in Table A.I is based. Standard deviation — a statistical measure of variability. Sl — the standard deviation of the modulus of rupture found in the sample. S2 — the standard deviation of the modulus of elasticity found in the sample. Site number (Site no.) — the site or pole yard from which the sample was obtained (see Table A.2). For some sites, additional identifying information can be found in the applicable document referenced in Clause A.9. Treatment — the code (see Clause A.8) describing the conditioning and treatment of poles before strength testing. Note: Further information can be found in the applicable document referenced in Clause A.9.

clause_list.title: Strength determination
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: A reasonable estimate of the percentage of a sample of poles having strengths falling within a specific range can be obtained using normal probability theory. On this basis, the range expressed by ± 1 standard deviation from the average value will Include about 68% of cases, ± 2 standard deviations from the average will include about 95% of cases, and ± 3 standard deviations from the average will include about 99.7% of cases. Thus, from a sample of poles having an average modulus of rupture of 552 bar (8000 psi) and a standard deviation of 69 bar (1000 psi), the strengths of 68% of the sample can be expected to fall within the range of 483 to 621 bar (7000 to 9000 psi), 95% within the range of 414 to 690 bar (6000 to 10 000 psi), and 99.7% within the range of 345 to 758 bar (5000 to 11 000 psi).

clause_list.title: Coefficient of variation
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: If a coefficient of variation for any sample is desired, it may be calculated by expressing the appropriate standard deviation as a percentage of the average value.

clause_list.title: Sample exclusions
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: Some samples in Table A.I have been excluded from the weighted species averages in the rows labelled "Average" because they were considered extraordinary on account of length, kerfing, treatment, moisture content, or decay.

clause_list.title: Moisture content
clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: The moisture content of most specimens when tested was above the fibre saturation point, as required by ASTM [)1036, which has been used since 1949 for the testing of utility poles. The fibre saturation point is the moisture content level at which swelling of the wood ceases or shrinkage begins. A moisture content above the fibre saturation point is a condition at the groundline recognized as the best approximation for the purposes of this Standard.

clause_list.section: Annex A (informative) Database for classification stresses
clause_list.text: Further information on the samples listed in Table A.I and on the derivation of the numbers in that Table is archived at Forintek Canada Corp.

Some of the samples were tested in the green condition or in a condition of moisture content greater than the fibre saturation point. Other samples were seasoned and then butt soaked before they were tested for bending strength.

clause_list.title: Derivation
clause_list.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles

clause_list.title: Calculation of minimum circumferences and horizontal loads
clause_list.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
clause_list.text: The minimum circumferences specified in Tables 4 to 13 have been calculated in order for each species in a given class to develop groundline stresses approximately equal to those specified in Table 3 when a given horizontal load is applied 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top of the pole. The horizontal loads used in the calculations for separating the thirteen classes are specified in Table B.I.

clause_list.title: Cantilever groundline stress assumptions and taper calculation
clause_list.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
clause_list.text: In making the calculations, it was assumed that the pole is used as a simple cantilever and that the maximum fibre stress in the pole subjected to the bending moment applied will occur at the groundline. The circumference at the groundline was calculated using the standard engineering formula. This value was then used to calculate the required circumference 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt using a calculated taper per foot of length between the groundline and 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt. The calculated circumference 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt was rounded to the nearest 13 mm (1/2 in). Note: A calculated taper is the difference between the minimum top circumference and the groundline circumference divided by the length between them.

clause_list.title: Theoretical groundline vs above groundline maximum stress
clause_list.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
clause_list.text: The assumption that the maximum fibre stress in the pole occurs at the groundline is theoretically correct, provided that the circumference at the groundline is not more than 1-1/2 times the circumference at the point of loading. If the circumference at the groundline is more than 1-1/2 times the circumference at the point of loading, theoretically the maximum fibre stress in the pole occurs above the groundline at the point where the circumference is 1-1/2 times that at the point of loading (not necessarily the circumference 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top). When the load is not applied 0.61 m (2 ft) from the top, it is necessary for the class of pole to be determined by making separate calculations from the specific loads to be supported. Unless other information is available to substantiate the actual taper of the pole for a given species, these calculations should be based on the taper determined by the difference in circumference between the specified top dimension and the groundline dimension divided by the distance in feet between the two measurements.

clause_list.title: Shrinkage
clause_list.section: Annex B (informative) Classification procedure for poles
clause_list.text: The dimensions specified in Tables 4 to 13 are the minimum dimensions of the poles when offered to the purchaser, regardless of the state of seasoning. While it is recognized that some shrinkage will occur in seasoning, it is known that the dimensional loss is offset by an increase in fibre strength. Class H3 H2 HI

clause_list.section: Annex C (informative) Classification procedure for reinforcing stubs
clause_list.text: Length of associated poles, ft 20, 25, 30 35, 40 45, 50 60, 70 It is recognized that a pole will be stub reinforced usually after it has served a substantial part of its physical life. Consequently, a stub should have a life at least equal to the remaining life of the pole. Experience has indicated that this result will generally be met by selecting a reinforcing stub whose circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt is approximately 51 mm (2 in) less than the circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt of a new replacement pole adequate to support the load. For example, a 3.05 m (IO ft) Class Z stub is designed to develop the expected remaining strength of a 9.1 (30 ft) Class I pole.

clause_list.title: Application
clause_list.section: Annex E (informative) SI (metric) versions of Tables 1 to 23
clause_list.text: Tables E.I to E. 23 provide Sl (metric) equivalents for Tables 1 to 23. The dimensions specified in Tables 4 to 23 have been converted to Sl units in Tables E.4 to E.23 by recalculating the theoretical circumference at 1.83 m (6 ft) from the butt in yard/pound units. The results have then been converted to centimetres and rounded to the nearest centimetre. This is thought to be more accurate than converting the values in Tables 4 to 23, which are rounded to the nearest 13 mm (1/2 in). In cases of dispute, the dimensions specified in Tables I to 23 should govern.
